This is a review of a task, not the task itself. Do not do the clinical work. You have only read tools: there is no write tool and no finish tool.

Below is the instruction an agent receives for task contrast-ct-prep. Read it, then use the read tools to read everything it depends on: the clinic policies it names or that govern it (read_policy), the patients, orders, results, notes and inbox items it points at, and your own context (get_context).

Report every ambiguity you find, where a careful clinician could not tell what the task wants:
- two_readings: a sentence of the instruction or a policy reads two ways, and the two readings lead to different actions;
- missing_fact: a fact the work needs (a date, a dose, a threshold, a recipient, a patient) is not in the instruction, the policies or the chart;
- conflict: two sources (the instruction, a policy, a note, an order, a result) say different things about the same point.

Quote the exact words each finding rests on. Leave out what is only hard, long or clinically unusual but has one reading. If you find none, say so with an empty list.

End with one final message that holds only this JSON object, with no text before or after it:
{"findings": [{"kind": "two_readings" | "missing_fact" | "conflict", "source": "<instruction, or the policy id, or the resource as Type/id>", "quote": "<the exact words>", "readings": ["<what one reading asks the agent to do>", "<what another asks>"], "explanation": "<why a careful clinician could not tell which is meant>"}]}
Give readings two or more entries for two_readings and conflict, and none for missing_fact.

<instruction>
Please place the contrast CT for Daniel Ferreira for his Monday 10/26 9:00 slot and handle the prep RBC-RAD-07 requires, including telling him what to do.

— Dr. Okafor

</instruction>

content.text:
RBC-RAD-07 Contrast CT preparation

Applies to scheduled outpatient CT with intravenous iodinated contrast that the clinic orders.

§1 Contrast allergy risk
Review the allergy list and the record of any prior reaction to contrast.
The risk factor is a prior allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast medium.
Allergies to shellfish, to povidone-iodine or other topical iodine, and to unrelated drugs or foods are not risk factors for a contrast reaction.

§2 Prior mild or moderate allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast
Adapted from the ACR Manual on Contrast Media, elective prednisone-based premedication.
Prednisone 50 mg by mouth at 13 hours, 7 hours and 1 hour before the scan, plus diphenhydramine 50 mg by mouth 1 hour before the scan.
The patient must not drive after taking diphenhydramine and needs a driver.

§3 Prior severe allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast
No iodinated contrast. Consult the radiologist.

§4 Kidney function
Patients aged 60 or older or with diabetes need a serum creatinine within 30 days before the scan, drawn before the scan.

§5 Orders
Link the imaging order to its appointment.

Telephone note - Riverbend Family Medicine
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast booked at St. Brigid Imaging for Monday 10/26 at 9:00 AM (arrive 8:45). Called the patient to confirm the time.
He asked whether he needs to do anything before the scan. Told him Dr. Okafor will place the order and send him instructions.

Jordan Reyes, NP

Telephone note - Riverbend Family Medicine
Letter from GI (St. Brigid Regional) received: the 1.3 cm pancreatic body cyst seen on CT in June 2023 is overdue for surveillance imaging. GI had asked for repeat imaging in 2024; the referral was not completed. GI recommends CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast, pancreatic protocol.
Called the patient. We discussed MRI as an alternative; he is claustrophobic and prefers CT, which GI accepts. Sent to scheduling to book at St. Brigid Imaging.
Type 2 diabetes: continues metformin 1000 mg twice daily; no new symptoms.

Maya Okafor, MD

St. Brigid Regional - Radiology Report
Patient: Daniel Ferreira   DOB 1962-03-30
Exam: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast   Date: 2023-06-20

Indication: left lower quadrant pain; history of sigmoid diverticulosis.
Technique: axial CT of the abdomen and pelvis after 100 mL iohexol (Omnipaque 350) IV. The patient was premedicated for a prior contrast reaction; no reaction today.

Findings: mild sigmoid diverticulosis without diverticulitis. A 1.3 cm well-circumscribed cystic lesion in the pancreatic body, without a solid component, wall thickening or main duct dilatation. Liver, spleen and kidneys are unremarkable.
Impression:
1. No diverticulitis.
2. 1.3 cm cystic lesion of the pancreatic body, likely a side-branch IPMN. Recommend surveillance imaging; GI referral.

Radiologist: Tunde Adeyemi, MD

St. Brigid Regional - Radiology Report
Patient: Daniel Ferreira   DOB 1962-03-30
Exam: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast   Date: 2019-05-14

Indication: right lower quadrant pain for 3 days.
Technique: axial CT of the abdomen and pelvis after 100 mL iohexol (Omnipaque 350) IV.

Findings: normal appendix. Sigmoid diverticulosis without inflammation. Liver, pancreas, spleen, adrenal glands and kidneys are unremarkable. No free fluid.
Impression: no acute abnormality. Uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulosis.

Contrast reaction: about 5 minutes after the injection the patient reported itching and developed diffuse hives over the trunk and all four limbs, with mild swelling of both eyelids. No throat tightness, no hoarseness, no dyspnea, no wheeze. BP 132/84, HR 92, SpO2 98% on room air. Diphenhydramine 50 mg given IV. The hives and eyelid swelling faded over 90 minutes; observed for 2 hours and discharged.
Classification: moderate allergic-like reaction to iohexol. Added to the allergy list.

Radiologist: Tunde Adeyemi, MD

Given a moderate reaction history, I'm mapping out the premedication schedule for the Monday 9:00 scan—prednisone doses at 20:00 Sunday, 02:00 and 08:00 Monday, plus diphenhydramine at 08:00, and noting the patient will need a driver. I also need to check for a recent creatinine before the scan since none is on file, so I should order labs today or over the weekend, while metformin isn't addressed by policy so no hold is needed there. I'm trying to recall whether ACR guidance specifies anything I'm missing.

Actually metformin doesn't need to be held unless eGFR is below 30 or there's acute kidney injury—since policy stays silent on it, that's just general knowledge rather than a true ambiguity. I should go back and check the other policies for communication, lab requirements, and metformin guidance, plus the catalog.

entries.source: Environment-local policy. §2 adapted from the ACR Manual on Contrast Media, Version 2026 (acr.org, https://www.acr.org/Clinical-Resources/Clinical-Tools-and-Reference/Contrast-Manual, captured 2026-10-24; Chapter 4 'Patient Selection and Preparation Strategies Before Contrast Medium Administration' unchanged since 2017 per the Manual's version history), 'Specific Recommended Premedication Regimens', Elective Premedication option 1: '50 mg prednisone by mouth at 13 hours, 7 hours, and 1 hour before contrast medium administration, plus 50 mg diphenhydramine intravenously, intramuscularly, or by mouth 1 hour before' (verified); adapted: the clinic uses option 1 only, by mouth, and keeps diphenhydramine, which the Manual calls optional. The 2025 ACR-AAAAI consensus (Wang et al., Radiology 2025;315(2) and J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2025;13:1029-1047) recommends no premedication after a mild reaction, says premedication may be considered after a moderate one, and recommends switching to a different contrast agent when feasible; the clinic keeps the Manual's premedication for mild and moderate reactions and does not require a switch, and the task's reaction is moderate. §1 from the same chapter: 'Patients with shellfish or povidone-iodine (e.g., Betadine) allergies are at no greater risk from iodinated contrast medium than are patients with other allergies' (verified). §3 stricter than the Manual, which calls a prior severe reaction 'a relative contraindication' (verified). §4 environment-local: the Manual's Post-Contrast AKI chapter lists diabetes as an optional reason to check renal function and says 'Some accept a 30-day interval in outpatients' (verified); the age 60 trigger is local. §5 environment-local.
